https://www.dw.com/en/woman-life-freedom.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MdL9 The protests brought 'fundamental' changes to Iran, an activist told DW Image: Anonymous/Middle East Images/IMAGO Advertisement On September 16, 2022, Jina Mahsa Amini , a 22-year-old Kurdish woman, died away in a Tehran hospital . She had left her home in northwestern Iran to visit the capital and was then confronted by Tehran's morality police , who claimed the she was violating the mandate for women to cover their hair. The police arrested her. Three days later, she was declared dead . For many Iranians, the brutality of law enforcement officers toward women accused of violating hijab rules was nothing new. And yet, Amini's death triggered an unprecedented outpouring of anger. Protesters all across the country took to the streets under the slogan "Woman, Life, Freedom." They marched for months , but the regime eventually managed to suppress the movement with a violent clampdown. "From my perspective, the movement 'Woman, Life, Freedom' is the biggest social and cultural change in Iran in decades," the writer, poet and activist Pouran Nazemi told DW. Iran uprising seen through the eyes of Iranian women To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Nazemi's work as a women's rights activist has gotten her arrested several times in recent years. Still, she refuses to be intimidated. She said the movement had clear goals right from the start: ending the hijab mandate and ending state violence against Iran's population. Though those goals were ultimately not met, the protests did lead many people to recognize their own power within the society. "The institutions still use physical violence and occasional arrests against us," Nazemi said. "But something fundamental has changed." Hijab law still under debate Even now, amid the ongoing war with the United States , parts of the Iranian regime are still focusing on the hijab mandate . Many politicians are supporting a new bill which would introduce significantly stricter punishments for women violating the hijab order in public places. One lawmaker described the missing head coverings as a "deep wound in the body of society." Iranian women unveiled: A shift in hijab enforcement? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The proposed law has been in limbo for years and marked by wrangling between various state institutions. I a virtual parliamentary session on September 6, several lawmakers urged Parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf to pass the proposed legislation to the president for signing. New normal for young Iranians A 17-year-old female student told DW that she doesn't even think about wearing a hijab in public. Like many other young women , the pupil is posting pictures and videos of herself in colorful skirts and summer clothing on social media. To her, this is the new normal. "My mother is not wearing a hijab either," the student said. "She is still a bit afraid and always carries a scarf so she can cover up in an emergency." Even this degree of freedom would be hard to imagine just a few years ago. It was only after the 2022 protests that many woman started openly defying the government regulations and deciding for themselves if they wanted to cover up. Decades of female resistance Iranian women's resistance to the regime did not start with the "Woman, Life, Freedom" protests. An important phase in the long history of dissidence played out 20 years ago, the women's rights activist and writer Mansoureh Shojaee told DW. Along with other Iranian activists and feminists, Shojaee started the "One Million Signatures" campaign in 2006. The goal was for a million people to sign a petition to change laws that discriminate against women. This campaign became an important role model for feminist activism and societal mobilization in Iran. Activists went into the streets — and to universities, neighborhoods and private homes. They talked to people about divorce, custody, inheritance, court testimony, and polygamy. They also set up workshops, study groups and other cultural and media events. Nobel Prize winners among activists facing repression From the very beginning, the initiative was met with massive state repression. Activists were summoned by the police, arrested and dragged through courts. In the years that followed, authorities raided and shut down a rights NGO run by Shirin Ebadi , a lawyer and advocate for women and children who in 2003 became the first Iranian to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Ebadi's deputy at the Defenders of Human Rights Center, Narges Mohammadi — the winner of the 2023 Nobel Peace Prize — was arrested multiple times over the years. The women's rights activist and journalist Mansoureh Shojaee fled the country in 2011, as have many dissidents over the years. Fleeing Iran for freedom To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Shojaee now lives in the Netherlands. The activists never met their goal of reaching 1 million signatures. Still, they managed to change the conversation about the legal and social position of women. For this reason, Shojaee does not see the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement as a full-on break with the past, but only as one of the chapters in the much longer story of Iran's resistance. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/pm-.text: The Budapest Times PM says national interests prevailed on all key issues at EU summit Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar expressed his satisfaction on Friday in Brussels, as — according to a video message he shared on his social media page — at the two-day EU summit "we achieved success on every issue important to our country," with Hungarian interests prevailing on every key question. In his message, Péter Magyar stressed that although he is feverish and tired at the tenth hour of the second day of the EU leaders’ summit in Brussels, he is satisfied with the results achieved. “Veteran, experienced prime ministers” said that there had not been such an open, candid, and at times emotional debate in Brussels in years. There was everything: veto threats, shouting, alliances, and enormous disputes, he said. “But most importantly: after two days of extraordinarily intense negotiations, I was able to stand up proudly knowing that Hungarian interests prevailed on every important issue,” Péter Magyar stressed. Regarding the migration debate at the EU summit, the prime minister emphasised that by now everyone can see that the previous flawed, permissive policy cannot be continued, as mass migration poses serious social, economic, and security risks across Europe. He stated that on behalf of Hungary, he supported the position of the member states calling for the strictest possible action — the Visegrád Four, as well as Italy, Denmark, and Belgium. He said he described it as completely unacceptable in the debate that Hungary must pay a daily fine of one million euros for defending its own and Europe’s external borders. He reported that he had received a promise from both member states and the President of the European Commission to resolve the relevant EU court case. According to him, the “toughest and longest debate” at the EU summit was triggered by energy policy, which he said poses a threat to the competitiveness of the European Union. “More and more people feel that the current regulations would impose unbearable burdens in the future — not only on European industry and businesses, but on the population as well,” he stressed. “This is not acceptable for us — for the Visegrad Four and many other member states. In a tough debate lasting hours, as part of a broad coalition, together with the V4 member states, Italy and Greece, we managed to ensure that the European Union reassess the social and economic impacts of the adopted regulations,” said Péter Magyar, adding that this was an extremely important breakthrough in the fight against high energy prices. He recalled that on the Friday of the summit he held one-on-one talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, during which — as he emphasised — he welcomed the political agreement reached between Hungary and Ukraine on strengthening the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia. He confirmed to the Ukrainian president that, as a first step toward restoring mutual trust, Hungary greatly appreciates the fact that, under the agreement, Ukraine’s parliament passed the minority education law, and that the Ukrainian side immediately began implementing it. “I expressed my gratitude for the Ukrainian parliament’s September resolution, in which they acknowledged that crimes were committed against the ethnic Hungarians of Transcarpathia between 1944 and 1946 through the forced deportation to labour camps and mass deportations,” he said. He said he agreed with the Ukrainian president to continue consultations between the two countries at ministerial level, with particular attention to be paid to further improving the situation of minorities. “We agreed that it is in the interest of both countries to place political and economic relations on new foundations,” he stated, adding that he had assured the Ukrainian president of his full solidarity in light of the “inhuman Russian aggression” waged against his country for nearly five years. Hungary is ready to provide assistance through every possible diplomatic means to bring about an early ceasefire and a lasting peace, he emphasised. He also reported that, on the occasion of the European summit, he had held talks with the leaders of the European People’s Party (EPP) and of member states “advocating stricter EU migration rules.” In the course of these discussions, he made it clear that Hungary would only accept the EU’s new seven-year budget in December if Hungary received all the development funds it is entitled to, and if the EU funds allocated to the common agricultural policy and cohesion development were not reduced by any amount. “We have just come through an important, substantive EU summit, which showed that — without vetoing and by building genuine alliances — we are able to represent the interests of the Hungarian people and Hungarian businesses far more effectively than before,” said Péter Magyar, who then informed the public that on Saturday, the ministers of the Tisza government would continue finalising Hungary’s 2027 budget.
